subject: Cloud Computing
title: Serverless Databases
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Serverless Databases.

hook.text: Traditional databases run 24/7, even if nobody's querying them. Serverless databases wake on demand.

buildup.text: Services like Aurora Serverless and Neon scale to zero — literally costing nothing when idle.

discovery.text: They scale up automatically when queries arrive and scale back down when activity stops.

twist.text: Scale-to-zero has a cold start problem too. The first query after idle time can be painfully slow.

climax.text: Serverless databases are perfect for dev environments and bursty workloads. Less so for constant traffic.

punchline.text: Pay nothing when idle. Pay more when busy. That's the deal.

quiz.question: What does 'scale to zero' mean for serverless databases?
options: The database shuts down when idle and costs nothing until the next query
The database deletes all data when not in use
Storage capacity shrinks to zero bytes automatically

details.summary: Serverless databases auto-scale capacity and charge per query or operation rather than provisioned resources. Services like DynamoDB on-demand, Aurora Serverless, and Firestore eliminate database sizing decisions and idle costs entirely.
details.whyItMatters: Traditional databases require capacity planning that either wastes money through over-provisioning or risks outages from under-provisioning. Serverless databases solve both problems.
takeaways: Capacity auto-scales based on actual query demand
Billing per operation eliminates idle resource waste
No need for capacity planning or instance sizing

faq.question: Are serverless databases cost-effective at scale?
faq.answer: For variable workloads, serverless databases often cost less than provisioned capacity. For steady, high-throughput workloads, provisioned capacity with reserved pricing is typically cheaper. The break-even point depends on traffic patterns and volume.

faq.question: What are the limitations of serverless databases?
faq.answer: Connection limits, cold start delays on idle databases, fewer configuration options, and potentially higher per-query costs at sustained high volume are limitations. Some serverless databases also lack features available in their provisioned counterparts.
